read.sections.0.heading.source: The street is part of the architecture
read.sections.0.heading.back: The street is part of the architecture

read.sections.0.text.source:
A building's front door connects private space to a wider street. Shops, paths, windows and entrances affect how people work, move and live near one another. A street is public space: space used by a wider community. So we can study architecture at the scale of one building and at the scale of a neighbourhood.

In George Town, Malaysia, shophouses are an important part of the historic town. A shophouse is a building that combines a business and a home. Traditionally, the business was below and the housing above. Shophouses are often narrow and long, and they stand in rows with shared walls. Airwells, open spaces inside the building, bring light and fresh air into deep rooms. Covered walkways, called five-foot ways, shelter people as they move along the fronts. A shop meets customers at the street, and an airwell deals with heat and light inside. These links connect a building's form with daily use.
read.sections.0.text.back:
A building's front door connects private space with the wider street. Shops, paths, windows and entrances affect how people work, move and live close together. A street is public space: space used by the wider community. So we can study architecture at the scale of one building and at the scale of a neighbourhood.

In George Town, Malaysia, shophouses are an important part of the historic town. A shophouse, or ruko, is a building that combines a business and a home. Usually, the business is below and the home above. Shophouses are often narrow and long, and stand in rows with shared walls. Airwells, that is, open spaces inside the building, bring light and fresh air into the deep rooms. Covered walkways, called five-foot ways or kaki lima, shelter people walking along the fronts. A shop meets buyers at the street, and an airwell deals with heat and light inside. These links connect a building's form with daily use.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Shophouse" is "rumah toko" (glossary word), with "ruko" as a form, the word Jakarta learners use every day. "Five-foot way" is kept and given as "kaki lima": the Indonesian and Malay "kaki lima" (as in "pedagang kaki lima") comes from this walkway. "Airwell" is "sumur udara", flagged: architects may say "void" or "sumur cahaya".

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A front door joins a home to the street. Shops, paths, windows and doors shape how people work and live close together. A street is public space. That means it is a space for everyone. So we can study one building or a whole neighbourhood.

George Town is a city in Malaysia. It has many old shophouses. A shophouse is a shop and a home in one building. The shop was downstairs and the home was upstairs. Shophouses are narrow and long. They stand in rows and share walls. An airwell is an open space inside the house. It lets in light and fresh air. Covered paths run along the front. They give shelter to people walking past. They are called five-foot ways. Each part links the building to daily life.

read.sections.1.heading.source: George Town: a port of many connections
read.sections.1.heading.back: George Town: a port with many connections

read.sections.1.text.source:
George Town grew as a British colonial port from the late eighteenth century. Its trade networks linked the Malay Archipelago, India, China, the Middle East and Europe. Malay, Chinese, Indian and European connections appear in the town's buildings and in practices that continue today. Places of worship, languages, festivals and neighbourhoods keep more specific histories within those broad labels. "Multicultural" describes these lives that met and mixed. It does not mean that each community arrived at the same time, shared one identity, or held equal political power under colonial rule.

Shophouses make this exchange easy to see. The local heritage organisation identifies early use by Indian and later by Chinese migrants, followed by changes involving European building experts. Owners redesigned façades, the fronts of buildings that face outwards, while keeping the mix of shop and home. The row in the photograph belongs to a history of change, not to one pure style from one homeland. A decorated front alone cannot tell us every builder's background or who lives there now.
read.sections.1.text.back:
George Town grew as a British colonial port from the late 18th century. Its trade networks connected the Malay Archipelago, India, China, the Middle East and Europe. Malay, Chinese, Indian and European connections appear in the town's buildings and in customs that continue today. Places of worship, languages, festivals and neighbourhoods keep more specific histories behind those broad labels. "Multicultural" describes these lives that met and mixed. The label does not mean that each community arrived at the same time, had one identity, or had equal political power under colonial rule.

Shophouses make this exchange easy to see. The local heritage organisation records early use by Indian migrants and later by Chinese migrants, then changes involving European building experts. Owners redesigned façades, that is, the fronts of buildings that face outwards, while keeping the mix of shop and home. The row in the photo is part of a history of change, not one pure style from one homeland. A decorated front alone cannot tell us every builder's background or who lives there now.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Chinese" (people) is "Tionghoa", as in Southeast Asia Through Time; "migrants" is "pendatang".

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
George Town grew as a British colonial port from the late 1700s. Ships linked it with the Malay world, India, China, the Middle East and Europe. Malay, Chinese, Indian and European links can be seen in its buildings. Places of worship, languages and festivals keep each group's own history. People call the town multicultural. But the groups did not all arrive at the same time. They did not share one identity. Under colonial rule, they did not have equal power.

Shophouses show this mixing. The local heritage group says Indian and then Chinese migrants used them early on. Later, European building experts changed them too. Owners changed the façades. A façade is the front of a building. But the shop and home stayed together. So the row in the photo shows change over time. A decorated front cannot tell us who built it. It cannot tell us who lives there now.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
George Town grew as a British colonial port from the late 1700s. Ships connected it with the Malay world, India, China, the Middle East and Europe. Malay, Chinese, Indian and European connections can be seen in its buildings. Places of worship, languages and festivals keep each group's history. People call the town multicultural. But the groups did not arrive at the same time. They did not have one identity. Under colonial rule, their power was not equal.

Shophouses show this mixing. The local heritage group says Indian and then Chinese migrants used them first. Later, European building experts changed them too. Owners changed the façades. A façade is the front of a building. But the shop and home stayed together. So the row in the photo shows change over time. A decorated front cannot tell us who built it. That front cannot tell us who lives there now.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Amsterdam: canals, trade and unequal wealth
read.sections.2.heading.back: Amsterdam: canals, trade and unequal wealth

read.sections.2.text.source:
For comparison, Amsterdam's canal district grew through a planned expansion of canals, streets, building plots and gabled houses, with shaped tops on their fronts. Its buildings also belong to a city network and to trade by sea. The photograph shows one part of that setting. It cannot prove each house's date, owner or first use.

Amsterdam's City Archives add a social history. Wealthy households lived on the wide canals, while craftspeople, shopkeepers and workers lived and worked in other streets. Some grand canal houses were paid for through trade in plantation goods produced by enslaved people. That link belongs in a story of trading wealth, even though the labour was far away and is missing from a handsome street view. It does not tell us how each pictured house was paid for.

The comparison connects buildings with work, movement, resources and unequal access to wealth. George Town's shophouses and Amsterdam's canal houses grew in different climates and political settings. Explaining these differences makes one shared question useful: how do trading streets organise private lives and wider connections? A street becomes clearer when we study its buildings and the people connected through them together.
read.sections.2.text.back:
For comparison, Amsterdam's canal district grew through a planned expansion of canals, streets, building plots and gabled houses, with shaped tops on their fronts. Its buildings are also part of a city network and of trade by sea. The photo shows one part of that setting. The photo cannot prove each house's building year, owner or first use.

The Amsterdam City Archives add its social history. Wealthy families lived along the wide canals, while craftspeople, shopkeepers and workers lived and worked in other streets. Some grand canal houses were paid for through trade in plantation goods produced by enslaved people. That link belongs in the story of wealth from trade, even though the work was done far away and does not show in a handsome street view. That link does not tell us how each house in the photo was paid for.

The comparison connects buildings with work, movement, resources and unequal access to wealth. George Town's shophouses and Amsterdam's canal houses grew in different climates and political settings. Explaining these differences makes one shared question useful: how do trading streets organise private lives and wider connections? A street becomes clearer when we study its buildings and the people connected through those buildings together.
read.sections.2.text.note: "Enslaved people" is "orang-orang yang diperbudak", as in Southeast Asia Through Time (never "budak" alone).

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Amsterdam is a city in the Netherlands. Its canal area was planned. People built canals, streets and tall houses with shaped tops. The houses were part of a trading city by the sea. The photo shows one part of it. It cannot tell us each house's date, owner or first use.

The city's records tell us more. Rich families lived on the wide canals. Workers and shopkeepers lived on other streets. Some big canal houses were paid for by trade in goods from plantations. Enslaved people were forced to grow those goods far away. That is part of the story. We just cannot see it in the street. But we do not know how each house in the photo was paid for.

The two cities had different weather and different rulers. In both, streets linked homes to trade. We understand a street better when we study its buildings and its people together.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
Amsterdam is a city in the Netherlands. Its canal area was planned. People built canals, streets and tall houses with shaped tops. The houses were part of a trading city by the sea. The photo shows one part of it. The photo cannot tell us each house's year, owner or first use.

The city's records tell us more. Rich families lived along the wide canals. Workers and shopkeepers lived on other streets. Some big canal houses were paid for by trade in goods from plantations. Enslaved people were forced to grow those goods in a faraway place. That is part of the story. We just cannot see it in the street. But we do not know how each house in the photo was paid for.

The two cities had different weather and different rulers. In both, streets connected homes with trade. We understand a street better when we study its buildings and its people together.

write.prompt.source: Explain one way a George Town shophouse connects home life with the street. Use two features from the reading.
write.prompt.back: Explain one way a George Town shophouse connects home life with the street. Use two features from the reading.

write.example.source: A shophouse has a shop on the ground floor. It opens onto the street, so customers walk in from the public space outside. It also has a covered five-foot way along the front. This path links it to the buildings next door and gives shelter to people walking past. Together, these connect the family's home upstairs with the busy street. The photo cannot show if each building is still used this way.
write.example.back: A shophouse has a shop on the ground floor. The shop opens onto the street, so buyers walk in from the public space outside. A shophouse also has a covered kaki lima along its front. This path connects it with the buildings next door and shelters people walking past. Together, these features connect the family's home upstairs with the busy street. The photo cannot show whether each building is still used this way.

visual.alt.back: A row of two-storey shophouses with orange tiled roofs. Upstairs, each house has three arched windows with wooden shutters, in pale green and blue plaster walls with moulded decoration. Downstairs are shop fronts and doors, one with a signboard in Malay and Chinese. A car and some motorcycles are parked in front.
